progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: series s01 (reading routine: verb, marks, content words and givens, constraint, tick each part), s02 (explain shows the link), s04 (assess needs a judgement with evidence; used in part d), s05 (values with units; consequential working). s07 is not assumed (in Biology it came earlier, after p02; in Chemistry its order relative to s06 is the Module 8 review's call), so s06 never relies on it. Biology: b11 (resistance by selection), p05 (zones of inhibition). Chemistry: Year 11 rates (gas volume against time levels off as a reactant runs out). Year 7 to 10 graphing (axes, plotting points) is assumed; the video names the HSC expectations on top of it. Students start Year 12.
progression.startsWith: Graph questions ask you to read, draw, describe or extend. The video opens: Graph questions look easy, which is why they're easy to lose marks on. Across the last twelve Chemistry and Biology marking feedback reports, eleven commented on graphs drawn or read poorly, and nine on trends described without the numbers. So here's how to read a graph, draw one that earns its marks, describe a trend with data, and know when you can extend the line.

teaching.task: When a question gives you data or asks for a graph, how do you read values with their units, draw a graph that earns its marks, describe the trend with numbers, and decide whether you can trust a value read beyond the data?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) graph questions look easy, yet most recent Chemistry and Biology marking feedback reports comment on graphs drawn or read poorly and on trends described without numbers (1); (2) read the axes first: what is measured, the units and what one small square is worth, then read across to the value with its unit (2); (3) one HSC-style Biology resistance question with four parts is set up (3); (4) part a, an even scale: years that jump by two then three must not be spaced evenly, or the trend bends (4); (5) label with units, a title, small crosses and one smooth line of best fit, not joined dots (5); (6) part b, describe the trend with direction and data, and say where any change happens (6); (7) percentage points and per cent give different numbers, so say which (7); (8) part c, interpolation reads inside the data from the line, with read-off lines drawn (8); (9) part d, extrapolation extends the line beyond the data and rests on an assumption that may not hold (9); (10) a line graph for continuous data or change over time, a column graph for categories (10); two drills, one per subject, with feedback (11 to 14); decision rule (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: graph questions look easy, which is why they are easy to lose marks on, and recent marking feedback keeps flagging graphs drawn or read poorly and trends described without numbers. The habit starts with the axes: what is measured, in what units and what one small square is worth, then axis to line to axis, writing the value with its unit. One HSC-style Biology question on E. coli resistance to an antibiotic is worked part by part. Part a builds an even scale even though the years jump by two then three, then labels, plots small crosses and draws one smooth line of best fit with the points scattered on both sides. Part b describes the trend with its direction and data, about one and a half percentage points a year, and then separates percentage points from per cent so the answer says which it means. Part c reads 2016 from the line, not the nearest point, which is interpolation; part d extends the line to 2040, which is extrapolation, and assesses the prediction by naming the assumption that the rate stays the same. A short contrast says when a column graph fits instead. Two drills follow, one per subject, with brief feedback that names the habit to drop, and a decision rule gathers read, draw, describe and extend.
teaching.openingDecision: Graph questions look easy, which is why they're easy to lose marks on. Across the last twelve Chemistry and Biology marking feedback reports, eleven commented on graphs drawn or read poorly, and nine on trends described without the numbers. So here's how to read a graph, draw one that earns its marks, describe a trend with data, and know when you can extend the line.
teaching.understandingCheck: the narration says "Do the one in your subject, or both". Drill 1, Chemistry, identify and explain, 3 marks: card: "A student measured the volume of carbon dioxide produced when marble chips reacted with excess hydrochloric acid. Her results and her graph are shown." Table: "Time (s) | 0 | 30 | 60 | 120 | 240"; "Volume of CO₂ (mL) | 0 | 22 | 38 | 55 | 62". The student's graph (coded): the five time values at equal spacing along the x-axis (0, 30, 60, 120, 240 equally spaced), the y-axis labelled "volume" with no unit, the points joined dot to dot with straight segments; a title is present. Demand: "Identify THREE problems with the student's graph and explain how to correct each. (3 marks)". Content: none beyond the card (rate slowing as the marble chips are used up is a grey tag only). Answer: uneven time scale (equal steps, for example every 30 s, with each time at its real position); y-axis without a unit (label "volume of CO₂ (mL)"); dot to dot (a smooth curve of best fit, through the origin, levelling off). Crossed habit: "a line of best fit must be a straight line" (best fit can be a smooth curve when the data curve). Drill 2, Biology, describe, 2 marks: card: "A student soaked paper discs (6 mm in diameter) in five concentrations of an antiseptic and placed them on agar spread with a harmless bacterium. After incubation she measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc (the zone of inhibition), including the disc. The table shows her mean results." Table: "Antiseptic concentration (%) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6"; "Mean zone diameter (mm) | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 16". Demand: "Describe the relationship between antiseptic concentration and zone diameter. (2 marks)". Answer: from 0% to 3% the zone diameter increased steadily as concentration increased, by about 3 mm per 1% (6 mm to 15 mm); from 3% to 6% it increased only slightly (15 mm to 16 mm), so it levelled off. Crossed habit: "As concentration increases, the zone increases." (no values; misses the change in pattern). Why these two: drill 1 tests drawing mechanics (three of the pack's listed faults: uneven scale, missing unit, dot to dot) on a curved data set, which also crosses the "best fit must be straight" habit; drill 2 tests description, the 9/12 fault, on a pattern that changes, so "direction, data, change" earns both marks. Each uses a context that viewers of its subject have met (Year 11 rates for Chemistry, p05 for Biology) but the card carries everything.
teaching.curriculumScope: No syllabus dotpoint (skills video, HSC exam skills series): the NESA glossary of key words (paraphrased) and the Working Scientifically skill Communicating (NSW Chemistry and Biology Stage 6 syllabuses, 2017). starts at "graph questions ask you to read, draw, describe or extend". Stops after reading a value with its unit; scale, labels, plotting and best fit (TAILS); describing with direction, data, change; interpolating with read-off lines; judging an extrapolation; line against column graphs; two drills.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. the shared skills kit (`src/explainer/lessons/skills-shared/`: `QuestionCard` with its annotation layer, `MarksBadge`, `AnswerBox`, `MarkCounter`, `WeakStrongPanel`, `RoutineStrip`, `DrillCountdown`, `Chip`, `GreyTag`, `CrossedHabit`, `PenArrow`, `Plate`, `Heading`, `HandLine`, `Flag`, `KeyNotes`, `Fade`), `BandLadder` from s04 and s05, and the graph parts from `src/explainer/lessons/chem-m6-c13/parts.tsx` (`Axes`, `Curve`, `GDot`, `Drop` for read-off lines, `Band`), imported, not copied (root may lift them to the shared kit). New lesson-local components (suggested folder `src/explainer/lessons/skills-s06`): `GridPaper`: a coded graph-paper rectangle (fine and bold lines, 20 by 15 squares) that the card's grid and the answer plots draw on. `ScaleTrap`: two small x-axes stacked: top, the five years at equal spacing (terracotta, "equal spacing: wrong"); bottom, the same years at real positions on an even 1-year scale (green). The five points plot on both: the top line visibly bends at 2014, the bottom stays straight. `TailsRail`: a five-row check card (T, A, I, L, S), rows lighting on cue, built like s07's `FixRail`, with a sixth row "line of best fit, not dot to dot". `TrendMove`: a three-row description card ("Direction", "Data", "Change"), mini and full states. `ExtendZone`: beyond the last data point, the line of best fit continues as a dashed grey line through a pale shaded region labelled "no data here"; on cue a small fan of three dashed possible paths (keeps rising, levels off, falls) opens from 2020, tag "the line assumes the top one". `ColumnMini`: a small column graph (three antibiotic categories, gaps between columns) beside a small line graph, for scene 9. Plates: listed under Assets (no new plates). No people, hands or faces.
